hints: Look at what atoms each polymer contains, since combustion products must come from those atoms plus oxygen.
Remember that poly(ethene) has only strong non-polar C-C and C-H single bonds with no reactive functional groups for microbes to attack.
Think about what happens in addition polymerisation, only the C=C double bond opens with no small molecule lost.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 - combustion of PVC**

PVC is poly(chloroethene), with repeat unit $-[\text{CH}_2-\text{CHCl}]-$. It contains C, H and Cl.

On burning in oxygen, C gives $\text{CO}$ and $\text{CO}_2$, H and Cl combine to give $\text{HCl}$ (plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$). So statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2 - disposal of poly(ethene)**

Poly(ethene) has a long saturated hydrocarbon chain with only strong C-C and C-H bonds.

There are no polar groups or hydrolysable links for bacteria or enzymes to break, so it is non-biodegradable and persists in landfill. So statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3 - empirical formula**

In addition polymerisation, $n$ monomer molecules join by opening the C=C bond:
$$n\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \rightarrow -[\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2]_n-$$
No atoms are lost and no $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is eliminated.

The repeat unit has the same atoms in the same ratio as the monomer, so the empirical formula is unchanged. So statement 3 is correct.

**Combine the conclusions**

All three statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct.

That corresponds to the option for 1, 2 and 3 together.

options.A: Correct, because all three statements are true. PVC gives CO, CO2 and HCl on combustion, poly(ethene) is inert to biodegradation, and addition polymerisation preserves the empirical formula.
options.B: Incorrect, because it includes only 1 and 2 and leaves out 3. Statement 3 is true since no small molecule is lost in addition polymerisation, so the monomer and polymer have the same empirical formula.
options.C: Incorrect, because it includes only 2 and 3 and leaves out 1. Statement 1 is true since PVC contains C, H and Cl, so combustion in oxygen can form CO, CO2 and HCl.
options.D: Incorrect, because it includes only statement 1. Statements 2 and 3 are also true. Poly(ethene) is non-biodegradable due to its unreactive saturated chain, and addition polymers retain the monomer empirical formula.
